name: PT AEP Pinago Plantations Tbk

frontmatter.title: AEP Pinago Plantations: a well-run mill with no float left to buy
frontmatter.summary: AEP bought control of this South Sumatra palm and rubber estate in 2026 and now holds almost all of it, leaving a stub float that cannot be traded. The business is a cash-generative CPO mill that buys most of the fruit it crushes, so its margin is a spread. The first half under the new owner brought a salary step-up no filing calls one-off: at that run rate the shares are worth less than the price, though not enough to sell.
thesis: The operating business is sound and cheap on cash: revenue of IDR2,303.9bn in FY2025 produced EBITDA of IDR489.5bn after restating the depreciation the data pack understates by roughly four-fifths [S3].

This is a mill more than an estate: 461 kt of FFB were crushed in FY2025 against 161 kt of own fruit, so two-thirds of the raw material is bought at a formula price and most of the CPO cost is a pass-through of the CPO price [S2].

Control changed hands in May 2026: AEP Plantations Plc bought 98.3% for 162 USD m at Rp3,600, ran a mandatory tender at a price a few per cent below it [S7], and the register now carries an insider stake of 99.5% with a free float of 0.5% [S6].

Our DCF values the equity at Rp3,612 a share against a price of Rp3,260, but the 30.0% liquidity discount the desk applies to a name trading 21,452,556 IDR a day takes the target to Rp2,808 - a HOLD with -9.8% total return [S0].

The variant view is on the cost base, not the price: H1-2026 salaries and allowances doubled and G&A plus selling annualise to a run rate the old sub-eight-per-cent assumption did not carry. That step-up, not the CPO deck, is what keeps the target below the price [S4].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited accounts - the first full year under AEP ownership, and the first test of whether the new parent changes the dividend or the cost base
AEP Plantations annual results - any statement of intent for the Indonesian asset (integration, offtake, a take-private or tender at a higher price)
El Nino harvest window - GAPKI has guided to a multi-million-tonne loss of national output in 2027, which would show in Q1-Q2 FFB intake
B40 to B50 biodiesel mandate progress, the main structural support for the domestic CPO reference price

blocks.text: **Rating HOLD; target Rp2,808 against a price of Rp3,260, a total return of -9.8% including the dividend.** The fundamental value of the business is above the price before the liquidity adjustment: our DCF, run on the house CPO deck and the deck's rupiah path, gives Rp3,612 a share and the method blend rolled forward one year at the cost of equity and net of the next twelve months' dividend is Rp4,012 [S0]. We then apply the desk's liquidity discount of 30.0% for a stock that trades about 21,452,556 IDR a day, and the target lands at Rp2,808, inside the band either side of zero that defines HOLD. That single path is the whole target: it is not blended with the scenario runs, for the reason section five sets out. The change from our initiation is the cost base, not the palm price: the first half under the new owner carries a run rate of salaries and general and administrative cost that is roughly four-fifths again the FY2025 ratio, and no note in the filing calls it one-off [S4]. Carrying it takes FY2026E net profit down by about a quarter and the target below the price - but by less than the ten per cent that would make this a REDUCE.

That discount is the whole story of this name. AEP Plantations Plc, a London-listed plantation operator, bought 98.3% of PT Pinago Utama Tbk in May 2026 for 162 USD m through its subsidiary AEP Nusantara Holdings, at Rp3,600 a share, and then ran the mandatory tender offer [S6]. The stake is now 99.5% and the free float is a fraction of one per cent, per the desk's IDX registry [S0]. The company now trades as PT AEP Pinago Plantations Tbk, per the same registry's updated name field; the annual report predates the change. A shareholder who buys today owns a sliver of a company whose controlling owner needs no minority capital and whose price is set by a handful of lots. The stock is a HOLD, not a REDUCE: the evidence on the current cost base puts the fundamental value below the price even before the structure is considered, but only just, and the structure removes any route to a re-rating rather than adding a fresh reason to sell. What would move us is a dividend set at the last-actual payout rather than the three-year average, which on its own takes the total return through the bottom of the HOLD band; section five shows that case.

What the company actually is matters for the value, and it is not a classic estate. In FY2025 the mill crushed 461 kt of fresh fruit bunches while the company's own nucleus estates produced 161 kt [S2], so roughly two-thirds of the raw material is bought from plasma smallholders and third-party growers at a formula price. That makes the P&L a spread business: most of the CPO cost moves with the CPO price and the smaller part is estate cost that moves with inflation. It is why the FY2025 margin held while the CPO price rose, and why our FY2027 forecast does not show the margin exploding on the deck's El Nino price spike.

The variant view is now on cost, and we say so plainly. We do not have a differentiated palm view: the house deck carries the GAPKI 2027 warning and we use it as given. Where we differ from the initiation is the operating cost: the H1-2026 LK shows salaries and allowances of IDR84.0bn, nearly double the prior-year line, a recurring cash line, and G&A plus selling of IDR131.1bn and IDR10.8bn on revenue of IDR1,116.6bn [S4]. That is a run rate, not a transaction cost, because no note or page of the filing discloses a one-off. The old sub-eight-per-cent assumption is what the initiation was built on, and it cannot survive the filing.

What moves the value: (i) whether the H1 cost step-up is permanent, which is the rating swing and which the FY2026 audited accounts will settle; (ii) the CPO price, which through the bought-fruit formula passes through at about two-thirds and therefore drives the spread; and (iii) the parent's capital-allocation decision, since a UK-listed owner may prefer to fund its own dividend from this asset rather than leave cash in it.

Small Indonesian plantation companies that end up as subsidiaries of larger listed groups usually stop being investable long before they are delisted: the shares keep trading, the price stops being informative, and the minority holder's only exit is the occasional tender. This is a structural feature of the market rather than a comment on any one company.

PT AEP Pinago Plantations Tbk, formerly PT Pinago Utama Tbk, is a South Sumatran oil palm and rubber producer based in Jakarta with estates in Musi Banyuasin regency [S4]. It was founded in 1994 as an agribusiness company managing oil palm and rubber plantations and listed on the IDX in 2019 under the PNGO ticker [S2]. The name changed after the 2026 change of control; the desk's IDX registry carries the new name and the annual report predates it. It operates a crude palm oil mill and a crumb rubber line, and it sells palm kernel, some traded fresh fruit bunches and compost alongside the two main products [S3].

**Segments and mix.** FY2025 revenue was IDR2,303.9bn [S0]. The revenue note splits it into crude palm oil, crumb rubber of IDR541.5bn, traded FFB and compost, with crumb rubber the only other material line [S3]. On our build CPO is about two-thirds of revenue and crumb rubber about a quarter, with palm kernel making up most of the balance. CPO sales volume was 106 kt at an average price of 14.1m per tonne; crumb rubber volume was 16.2 kt, down sharply on the prior year [S2]. Production was 105 kt of CPO from 461 kt of processed FFB [S2].

**The mill, not the estate, is the business.** Own FFB production was 161 kt against 461 kt crushed, so the mill runs substantially on bought fruit [S2]. This is a deliberate model: a nucleus estate of 19,952 ha hectares supports a mill that can pull fruit from the surrounding smallholder base, and the company earns a processing spread on the bought tonnes rather than an estate margin. It explains why the cost of sales is dominated by the FFB purchase line at IDR963.6bn, well above the estate's own harvest, processing, fertiliser and maintenance costs [S3]. It also explains the customer base: two Indonesian refiners, PT Sinar Alam Permai at 37.9% of revenue and PT MM QQ IKI, together took about three fifths of sales [S3].

**Strategy and footprint.** The estate is in one province and the company has not expanded geographically. Planted area rose from 19,147 ha hectares to 19,952 ha hectares in FY2025 [S2], a small increment consistent with ongoing replanting rather than a land-bank land grab. The palm nucleus is 11,797 ha hectares mature and 4,342 ha hectares immature, just over a quarter of it, so there is a young-palm pipeline inside the existing footprint [S2 p.88]; against it, a large block of the mature area is older than fourteen years and due for replanting, which is why we do not read the immature area as pure growth. The strategy disclosed in the annual report is productivity and quality-led market share in the core business; the sustainability section discusses emissions reduction, not a carbon-trading business [S2]. There is no published expansion plan, no new mill, and no acquisition programme for the company itself.

**Ownership and group.** Control passed to AEP Plantations Plc in May 2026: 98.3% acquired for 162 USD m, at Rp3,600/share a share, a mandatory tender, and a stake that now stands at 99.5% [S6, S0]. The company sits inside a UK-listed group that describes the deal as adding to its planted area and CPO output [S6]. For the minority holder this changes the governance question from "who is the family behind this" to "what does the parent want from it", which section six takes up.

**Market position.** With 19,952 ha hectares planted and 105 kt of CPO output, this is a small producer in an industry where the national crop runs to tens of millions of tonnes [S2]. It is a price-taker in every market it sells into and a price-taker in the FFB it buys; its position in the local catchment is its only real market power, because a smallholder within trucking distance of the mill has few alternatives.

**Size and growth.** Indonesia is the world's largest palm oil producer. GAPKI recorded national CPO production rising again in 2025, with palm kernel oil and domestic consumption both growing [S2]. The industry's growth in a given year is as much a weather outcome as an investment one. The structural demand driver is the biodiesel mandate: the annual report frames domestic consumption growth around the B40 programme and its successors, which puts a floor under the domestic reference price that this company sells at [S2].

**The 2027 supply shock.** On 11 November 2026 the GAPKI chairman said El Nino drought and fires could cut Indonesian palm output by up to three million tonnes, with the heaviest impact in the 2027 harvest, and asked the government for policy stability [S5]. That is the single most important industry fact for this name, and the house agri deck already carries it: the CPO benchmark rises to US$1,240/t in FY2027 before gliding back toward a long-run US$1,150/t [deck: d.agri.cpo]. The deck is the valuation input, not Yahoo: its basis is the World Bank Pink Sheet series, cross-checked against the Harga Referensi and the Bursa Malaysia FCPO strip, with MPOC guidance on the 2027 path [deck: d.agri.cpo]. The quoted FCPO strip rises through the first half of 2027 rather than falling - contango, not backwardation - and it is that rising curve, not a spot print, that the deck's FY2027 number is anchored on.

**Realisation and the domestic reference.** The single most important company-level industry fact is that an Indonesian mill sells at a domestic reference price, not at the exported benchmark. The export levy and duty are charged on the exporter at shipment, and no domestic sale bears them; no levy or duty line appears in the audited cost-of-sales note [S3]. That is why the audited FY2025 realised price of 14.1m per tonne converts to a ratio well above the like-for-like 2026 measurement against the old World Bank series; the wedge is structural and it is the same wedge the desk carries on its other Indonesian palm names [S3, S2].

**Competitive landscape and moat.** The industry is fragmented at the estate level and concentrated at the refinery level, and this company sits in the middle with one mill. Its moat is local: catchment, a working mill, and an established relationship with two refiners that take most of its output [S3]. There is no brand, no technology moat and no resource moat in the sense a miner has one - the palms are replaceable and the land is not scarce in South Sumatra. What it does have is a cost position that comes from throughput: spreading fixed mill cost over 461 kt kt of fruit is what makes the spread work, and losing bought-fruit supply is the real risk to the model.

**Five forces, briefly.** Supplier power is high and rising - smallholders can sell to any mill in the catchment, which is why the FFB purchase price tracks the CPO price so closely. Buyer power is high and concentrated in two customers [S3]. Threat of new entry is moderate: a mill is capital-intensive but not scarce. Substitution is a policy question, not a consumer one, and the biodiesel mandate is the substitute's friend. Rivalry is on price and logistics, and the price is set by the reference, so rivalry shows up as catchment competition for fruit rather than as discounting.

**External influences.** Three matter: the CPO price (the deck), the rupiah (the deck's path to Rp18,350/USD in FY2027 and a weaker long-run rate), and Indonesian policy on export levies and biodiesel [S0]. The macro desk's balance-of-payments-pressure regime and its commodity tilt are neutral for palm, so there is no macro overlay to add to the name beyond the deck.

Palm oil is the highest-yielding major oilseed per hectare, which is why Indonesia and Malaysia dominate the vegetable-oil trade, and why a supply shock in either country moves the global price rather than just the local one. The trade policy response - export taxes, levies and domestic-market obligations - has been a recurring feature of the market for two decades.

**Revenue build.** We model CPO as the priced line and the rest as a second block. Volume starts at 107.0 and rises to 113.0 by FY2030E: the nucleus has 4,342 ha hectares of immature palms, twenty-seven per cent of the planted area, which at the mature yield the estate already achieves would add roughly a seventh to own fruit at full maturity, but a large block of old palms is due for replanting at the same time and the bought-fruit catchment is not guided, so we take only about half the gross maturation [S2 p.88]. The mill is not the constraint: the acquisition report states a capacity of 120 t/h against the 461 kt of FFB it processed in FY2025 [S6]. Realisation is set at 0.76 of the deck benchmark, calibrated on the last twelve months rather than on the FY2025 audited ratio, for the reason set out in section two [deck: d.agri.cpo] [S3]. Non-CPO revenue is 809.7 IDR bn in FY2026E, held flat in real terms and grown only with inflation, at the reconciled gross margin of 40.8% [S3]. That block is mostly rubber, and rubber production has more than halved in two years, to 14,779 t in FY2025 [S2 p.90]; we will not grow a segment the annual report shows shrinking.

**Costs and margins.** The cost base is built from the FY2025 cost-of-sales note: bought FFB of IDR963.6bn, harvest and transport, processing, fertiliser and mature-plantation maintenance, all disclosed line by line [S3]. The shared estate lines are allocated between palm and rubber on the segment cost-of-sales evidence in the segment note, which shows the rubber segment carrying cost of sales close to nine tenths of its own revenue [S3 p.102]; because the non-CPO block had been carrying less cost than rubber alone, we moved the rubber share of the shared processing and estate cost out of the CPO pool. The resulting CPO cash cost is 11,509,000.0 IDR per tonne in FY2026E, of which the FFB purchase is the majority and moves with the CPO price while the estate cost moves with inflation [S3]. The result is an EBITDA margin that stays in the low twenties through the deck's price cycle instead of expanding with it, which is the correct behaviour for a tolling-style mill. SG&A is 12.3% of revenue, taken ex-depreciation so that the D&A line is counted once; that is the H1-2026 run rate, not the FY2025 audited ratio, because salaries and allowances rose to IDR84.0bn in the half year and no note discloses a one-off [S4].

**The cost base against the interim.** The half-year filing lets the curve be tested line by line. H1-2026 sales were IDR1,116.6bn, cost of goods sold IDR792.9bn, of which depreciation was IDR19.4bn and bearer-plant amortisation IDR13.7bn, and the bought-fruit line alone was IDR447.2bn [S4 p.7, p.85]. Cash cost of sales is therefore just over two-thirds of sales in the half, against IDR1,231.5bn of CPO cash cost plus IDR479.5bn of non-CPO cost on IDR2,431.4bn in FY2026E, a higher share by about two and a half points of revenue. The bridge has two parts, and neither is an unsourced cost step-up. The first is the second-half fruit price: the bought-fruit line is about two-thirds of the unit cost and is struck off the CPO reference, the first quarter's reference print ran below the deck's FY2026E average of USD 1,135 and the September spot ran above it [deck: d.agri.cpo], so the second half carries dearer fruit than the first. The second is a coefficient difference we disclose rather than smooth: the model's fruit line is the FY2025 audited cost per tonne re-priced by the deck, and the half's realised fruit cost per tonne of CPO runs a few per cent below that curve; because the interim does not disclose tonnage, the two cannot be split cleanly. The estate line, the only fixed component, escalates at the two-and-a-half per cent macro scalar. The resulting FY2026E unit cash cost is 11,509,000 rupiah a tonne against a first-half realised rate a few per cent lower, and annualising one half would import a seasonality assumption the filing does not support. We tested the alternative: holding the half's realised rate for the full year lifts FY2026E EBITDA by about a twelfth and the DCF by a few per cent, which leaves the rating unchanged. On margins, FY2026E EBITDA is IDR421.4bn on IDR2,431.4bn and FY2027E is IDR477.8bn on IDR2,706.2bn, against IDR489.5bn on IDR2,303.9bn in the last audited year; the half ran above both forecast years because its fruit was struck at the lower reference prints, while the last audited year, on the old cost base, ran above all of them.

**Earnings quality - the depreciation flag.** The data pack reports a FY2025 D&A charge that is the general-and-administrative allocation only. The fixed-asset note allocates a much larger depreciation charge to cost of sales and G&A, and a further bearer-plant amortisation sits in cost of sales [S3]. The restatement multiplies the pack's D&A several times over and lifts restated EBITDA to IDR489.5bn. The restated FY2025 EBITDA still excludes the bearer-plant amortisation, which sits inside cost of sales and is not added back; the forecast D&A line includes it. That definitional gap is about fourteen billion rupiah and is carried explicitly in the calibration reconciliation rather than hidden. The pack's EBIT was right - the charge was already deducted inside cost of sales - so the earnings were never overstated; only the EBITDA line and any cash-flow build that adds D&A back were understated. This is the standard direct-method artefact on IDX filings and it is restated here rather than modelled around.

**Accruals and cash conversion.** Non-financial, so the accruals ratio applies: (net profit - operating cash flow) / average total assets. Operating cash flow exceeded net profit in each of the last two years [S0], so the ratio is negative and there is no accruals warning. Cash conversion is strong because the working-capital cycle is short: receivables were a few days of sales at end-2025 against two concentrated refiners [S0]. Inventories are the larger item and reflect CPO and rubber stock, not slow-moving goods.

**Working capital and the balance sheet.** Working capital is 10.3% of revenue, the last actual rather than the three-year average, which is distorted by the 2022 inventory build [S0]. Net debt is small: debt fell through FY2025 and again by 30 September 2026, against a smaller cash balance, so net debt is roughly a tenth of EBITDA and there is no refinancing cliff [S0]. Equity of IDR1,166.7bn supports the book value per share you can rebuild from the model [S0].

**Capex and capital allocation.** FY2025 capex was IDR119.6bn, in line with the prior two years and dominated by immature planting, nursery and mill or vehicle replacement [S0, S2]. We hold it at the last actual in real terms; there is no announced expansion to fund. Dividends are the main use of cash: FY2025 declared DPS of Rp90, a payout of about a fifth of earnings, against a much higher payout the year before [S0]. The LK sets no fixed payout policy, leaving it to the annual meeting [S2], which is why we model the three-year average rather than the last year.

**Forecast shape.** Revenue grows with the deck's CPO path and the rupiah, peaking in FY2027 on the El Nino spike and settling back as the price glides to the long-run anchor. EBITDA follows the spread rather than the price, so it does not spike as hard; net profit falls in FY2026E because the SG&A run rate steps up against a modest price gain, then recovers with the deck. The first forecast year no longer looks like the last actual plus its own price move, and that is the finding: the H1-2026 cost base is different from FY2025, not a planning assumption we chose. FY2026E net profit is IDR255.8bn on revenue of IDR2,431.4bn [S0].

**Why this method set.** A plantation is a finite-life asset with a commodity price and a fixed cost base, so a life-of-asset DCF off a sourced price deck is the right primary method, and we give it seventy per cent of the weight. Multiples are a cross-check because a cyclical's current multiple is a statement about where we are in the cycle, not about value, and EV/EBITDA carries the other thirty per cent. We have dropped the P/BV leg rather than keep a number we do not believe: the multiple is the average of a peer median and a four-year own-history mean for a stock whose float has been thin for its entire listed life, so where it has traded tells us about the register, not about value. The report previously called that leg circular and kept fifteen per cent on it; that was inconsistent, and it is now gone [S0].
**Cost of capital.**

The build is the house deck's: a risk-free rate of 7.4% from the ten-year government bond, a mature equity risk premium of 4.2% and an Indonesian country risk premium of 2.5% from the Damodaran country file, an unlevered beta of 0.80 from the PLANTATIONS config (no measured regression exists for this name), relevered to 0.84 at the company's near-zero gearing, giving a cost of equity of 11.5% and a WACC of 11.2% [deck: m.rf_idr, m.erp_mature, m.crp_id]. The risk-free is the reviewed ten-year SUN yield in the macro deck, an observed government yield rather than an estimate. The cost of debt in the WACC is 9.4% pre-tax, which is the macro deck's risk-free rate plus its corporate debt spread: an rf-plus-spread default for an Indonesian borrower, not this company's realised rate. The realised rate is different and lower - the FY2025 interest charge of IDR29.8bn on opening debt works out at about five per cent - and that realised rate is what the interest line in the P&L carries; the two are stated separately so the file and the model cannot be read as disagreeing. At a debt weight of 6.3% the difference moves the WACC by about a tenth of a percentage point. Because net debt is trivial, the WACC is essentially the cost of equity and the valuation is not sensitive to the debt mix.
**Primary method.**

The explicit forecast runs ten years, which spans a replanting cycle; terminal growth is 2.5%, the macro deck's long-run Indonesian inflation, because the CPO deck's long run and the IDR cost base both escalate at that rate and real cash flow is flat [S0]. The terminal value is 47.7% of the DCF, which is normal for a name with a long explicit horizon and no depleting reserve. The DCF gives Rp3,612 a share. The method blend, 70.0% on the DCF and 30.0% on the multiple, is Rp3,717 today; rolled forward one year at the cost of equity and net of the next twelve months' dividend of Rp131, it is Rp4,012, and after the desk's 30.0% liquidity discount the target is Rp2,808. That chain, and nothing else, produces the published target.
**Cross-checks and divergences.**

EV/EBITDA at 6.0x gives Rp3,960 a share, 9.6% from the DCF. The label matters: the multiple is the average of the peer median and this stock's own five-year mean, as the industry config blends them, and the metric is the data pack's trailing LTM EBITDA, not a forward number. The pack's LTM EBITDA is on the same understated-D&A basis section three restates, so this leg is a floor rather than a fair comparison; on our restated forward EBITDA it would be higher. We show it as a cross-check on the market's starting point, not as a second valuation. There is no P/BV leg: it was dropped for the reason above, and the DCF and EV weights are renormalised to seventy and thirty.

**What the price implies.** The engine's reverse DCF is withdrawn. It solves for the deck multiplier that equates the DCF to the price, but the override mechanism it uses does not reproduce the base price path beyond the deck's explicit horizon (a multiplier of one returns a materially lower DCF than the base, which section five records as an engine defect outside this desk's edit rights). A number computed on a different price path from the valuation cannot be read against it, and we do not. What we can say without it is that the primary DCF, before the liquidity discount, is above the price while the DCF net of the discount is below it: the rating is driven by the discount and the cost base, not by a claim about the commodity.

**Sensitivity.** The engine's two-grid sensitivity table is withdrawn for the same defect: its CPO/FX grid is centred at a value that does not reproduce the base target, so every cell is off the valuation it purports to stress. Rather than publish a grid we cannot reconcile, we state the directions with the model's own arithmetic. The DCF is most sensitive to realisation and to the CPO long-run anchor, which enter revenue linearly and through the bought-fruit pass-through; a ten-percentage-point move in realisation moves the DCF by roughly a seventh; and the unit cost is the next lever, with the estate component now smaller after the rubber reallocation. Volume is a real lever too, not a rounding item, because the cost curve is per tonne and the bought fruit re-prices with the price; section five states the shocks in EBITDA terms rather than in a grid cell we cannot reconcile. The cost evidence in section three is the swing factor a sensitivity grid should be testing, and it is carried in the base case rather than in a cell.

**Ownership and float - the dominant risk (high likelihood, high impact).** With an insider stake of 99.5% and a free float of 0.5% [S0], there is no liquid market. The desk applies a 30.0% discount, and even that understates the problem for a real position: average daily traded value is about 21,452,556 IDR [S0], so a position of any size cannot be built or exited at the screen price. The risk is not that the business fails; it is that the exit does not exist. The exchange's minimum free-float rule is fifteen per cent, and the desk's IDX registry records this name short of it by about fourteen and a half percentage points, against a deadline of 31 March 2029. Meeting it means the parent placing or selling roughly a hundred and thirteen million shares - close to fifteen per cent of the capital and thousands of days of current turnover - or running a rights issue; either is a supply event inside the next two years. That cuts both ways: as an overhang it supports the discount we apply, and if the parent does place stock with institutions it is the one credible route to restoring a real float and closing that discount. The arm's-length transactions are on the record: the control block at Rp3,600 [S6] and the mandatory tender that followed at Rp3,584 [S7]. Our target sits below both, and section six reconciles why.

**Commodity price (medium likelihood, high impact).** CPO is the revenue line and the deck's El Nino spike cuts both ways: if it does not materialise, FY2027 revenue is materially below our base. The bear case prices the benchmark a fifth lower with the bought fruit re-priced down alongside it, and is set out in the scenario block below.

**Operational - the bought-fruit channel (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Two-thirds of the mill's raw material is bought [S2]. A competitor mill bidding up FFB in the catchment, or a smallholder replanting cycle that thins supply, cuts throughput and compresses the spread. No filing discloses the bought-fruit share by year, so this is the line we monitor least well.

**Regulatory and policy (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The domestic reference price, the export levy and the biodiesel mandate are all set administratively. A change to the levy changes the wedge between the domestic reference and the export print, which is the single largest assumption in our realisation ratio. A reversal of the B40 mandate would remove the structural bid under domestic prices.

**FX (low likelihood, medium impact).** Costs are rupiah, revenue is rupiah at a price set off a dollar benchmark, so a stronger rupiah cuts the realised price without cutting costs. The deck's rupiah path is the assumption; a sharp appreciation would compress the spread.

**Governance and parent behaviour (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The controlling shareholder has owned the asset for months. Related-party sales, an offtake arrangement with an affiliate, or a dividend policy set for the parent's needs rather than the subsidiary's would all be wealth transfers that the minority cannot block. See section six.

**Scenarios - stated as sensitivities, not weighted into the target.** The twelve-month target is the base case and nothing else: the method blend rolled forward at the cost of equity, Rp4,012, less the 30.0% liquidity discount, Rp2,808. The engine's shock override writes the CPO deck's long run flat beyond the last explicit year, so every stressed run sits on a lower price path than the valuation - a multiplier of one returns a materially lower DCF than the base. Blending those runs into the target would publish a number no model reproduces, which is the defect the previous draft carried and this one removes: the scenario table and both sensitivity grids are withdrawn, and the tail runs carry zero weight in the target. The model therefore holds the base at full weight; the likelihood we would assign in a computable engine is a quarter to each tail, stated here in words so the reader can see both. The states are described by their drivers, and they mirror each other: the CPO benchmark a fifth down or up, tonnes a twentieth down or up, and the bought-fruit line re-priced in the same shock at the model's own pass-through - which is what makes the shocks consistent with the base case, whose own unit cost rises with the price.

The bear is GAPKI's warning realised [S5]: the El Nino takes the 2027 crop and the benchmark gives back its spike, the mill runs below capacity on a thinner catchment, and the spread compresses because the bought fruit gets cheaper with the price while the estate cost does not. On the model's own cost formula that takes FY2027E EBITDA - IDR477.8bn on IDR2,706.2bn - down by roughly a third: the benchmark a fifth lower and tonnes a twentieth lower, with unit cost down by about a sixth because the bought fruit is the bulk of the cost and re-prices with the price while the estate cost does not. The bull is the same shocks the other way: the El Nino tightens the vegetable-oil balance into 2027, B40 toward B50 keeps the domestic bid firm, the mill holds its bought-fruit throughput and the extra tonnes convert into cash, and FY2027E EBITDA rises by roughly a third on the same arithmetic. We do not publish a per-share value for either tail, because the engine cannot compute one on the base price path; the direction is what carries weight, and the weight is on the base because the deck's own path already rises to an El Nino peak and falls back, while GAPKI's number is an industry aggregate rather than company guidance [S5]. The sharpest upside is not in the scenarios at all: a tender or take-private offer for the minority at the control price, Rp3,600/share, would make the float risk a realised gain rather than a discount.

**The dividend anchor.** We model a payout of 40.0%, the average of the three declared years, which produces a next-twelve-month dividend of Rp131 and the total return in the headline. The last dividend was declared by the previous owner, not by AEP: Rp90 a share on Rp412, a fifth of earnings, went ex on 15 January 2026 [S0], before AEP completed in May 2026 [S6], and the new owner has declared nothing since. That payment is the old owner's final distribution, not evidence of the parent's policy, so it neither supports nor undercuts the three-year average on its own: we keep the average because the parent's capital-allocation record is only months old and a single transition-year declaration is the least representative observation available. If the parent were to reset the payout to that level, the dividend line would fall by roughly a third and the total return would drop to around minus twelve per cent, through the bottom of the HOLD band into REDUCE territory. The reader should treat the payout, not the palm price, as the swing item between HOLD and REDUCE.

**Signposts that would change the view.** A tender or take-private offer at a premium to the current price would make the float risk a realised gain and move us to BUY. A guidance cut on bought-fruit intake or a loss of one of the two refinery customers would move us to SELL. A published parent-level plan to invest in the asset would raise the growth case; a dividend cut to fund the parent would lower it.

**Ownership and control.** AEP Plantations Plc holds 99.5% through AEP Nusantara Holdings, having bought 98.3% for 162 USD m in May 2026, at Rp3,600 [S6], and then run the mandatory tender for the remaining shares at Rp3,584 [S7]. That control price is the most recent arm's-length transaction for this asset and it is above both the November price and our target, so it needs an answer rather than an omission. The tender that followed ran at a price within a few per cent of the control block and was open for a maximum of 13.6 m shares million shares held by the public, a fraction of the paid-up capital [S7]; the parent's holding is now the registry insider figure and the residual free float is 0.5% [S0]. Nothing in the acquisition reporting says the tender is not a step to a delisting: we searched the source record and found no delisting undertaking from the parent, so the honest statement is that the listing survives for now with no commitment to keep it. The free float is 0.5% and the stock trades about 21,452,556 IDR a day [S0]; against the exchange's fifteen per cent minimum and the 31 March 2029 deadline recorded in the desk's IDX registry, the parent must place or sell a substantial block or run a rights issue (section five sizes it). The company's registered name changed after the deal closed, per the same registry; the annual report predates it. There is no pledge disclosure outstanding that we found, and no special-monitoring-board status or special notation letter in the source record.

**Why the target sits below the price the block cleared at.** The block price is what a buyer pays for control of the whole asset, including the right to set the dividend, direct the offtake and use the mill's cash; a minority share carries none of that [S6]. Our target is a minority value: the primary DCF, discounted for a float that is a fraction of one per cent and for the supply that restoring it will bring [S0]. The gap is the control premium and the liquidity discount, not a disagreement about the asset. If the parent ever offers to buy the minority, it should be expected to do so closer to the control price than to our target, and that is exactly why a tender is the sharpest upside catalyst in this file even as the shares are a HOLD at the screen price.

**Board and management.** The company reports a two-tier board with a board of commissioners and an audit committee, a nomination and remuneration committee, an internal audit unit and an external auditor, all disclosed in the annual report [S2]. Management continuity through the change of control is not disclosed; the first full year under the new owner will show whether the mill-level team stays.

**Related parties and concentration.** Trade receivables from related parties were carried alongside other related-party receivables and payables at end-2025 [S3]. The more important concentration is commercial rather than related-party: PT Sinar Alam Permai at 37.9% of revenue and PT MM QQ IKI at a further quarter, together about three fifths [S3]. We could not establish from the filings whether either customer is connected to the former controlling family; the notes list them as third-party customers with no related-party flag, and we treat them as third parties but flag the concentration as a governance-relevant dependency rather than evidence of a relationship.

**Audit.** The FY2025 accounts are audited and the audited statements were filed with the exchange [S3]. We found no qualification or going-concern reference in the material reviewed; the auditor's report is in the same filing and the Opinion section was not flagged by the scrubber.

**Dividend record.** Declared DPS has been volatile across the four years in the pack, from Rp130 to Rp90 [S0]. There is no fixed payout policy in the LK [S2]. For a minority holder the record is adequate but unpredictable, and the new owner's preference is unknown, which is why we model the average rather than the last year.

**ESG exposures.** The material issues are the ones every Indonesian planter faces: land tenure and HGU permits, deforestation and peat conversion in the catchment, fire and haze, labour standards for harvest crews and plasma smallholders, and the mill's effluent and methane capture. The company discloses a sustainability report alongside the annual report [S2] and the annual report describes the estates as nucleus plantations in Musi Banyuasin [S4]. We did not find a certification statement in the material reviewed, which matters commercially as much as ethically: European buyers increasingly require it, though this company's sales are domestic so the near-term revenue risk is limited.

**Dated catalysts.** The FY2026 audited accounts in early 2027 are the first full year under AEP ownership and the first read on whether the parent changes the dividend or the cost base [S2]. AEP Plantations' own results and any statement of intent for the Indonesian asset - integration, offtake, or a delisting or tender at a higher price - is the event that would change the float picture [S6]. The El Nino harvest window in the first half of 2027 is where GAPKI's warning either shows up in FFB intake or does not [S5]. Progress on the B40-to-B50 biodiesel mandate is the structural support for the domestic reference price [S2].

**KPIs we watch.** CPO sales volume and production, quarterly, against the flat 107.0 plan [S2]. The half-year general and administrative line, which at the H1-2026 rate sets the whole cost base; we want the FY2026 accounts to show whether the step-up in salaries persists [S4]. The bought-fruit share - 461 kt processed against 161 kt own in FY2025 - which is the operating lever no one guides [S2]. The realised price against the domestic reference, which is how we test whether 76% is still the right ratio. The two-customer concentration, which is the single largest non-price risk in the P&L [S3]. And the parent's cash policy: dividends declared, any related-party flows, any change in the stake, and any progress towards the minimum float before the 31 March 2029 deadline recorded in the desk's IDX registry.

**What would make us wrong.** If the current price is not a float discount but a genuine market view that the bought-fruit model is worth less than we think, then the bear case is the base case: on the arithmetic section five sets out, the benchmark a fifth lower and tonnes a twentieth lower take FY2027E EBITDA - IDR477.8bn on our base - down by roughly a third. That is the downside we state, in earnings terms, because the engine's shock override cannot be run on the base price path and we will not publish a per-share tail value we cannot reconcile. The test is the FY2026 accounts: if the mill's spread per tonne of CPO is materially below the FY2025 level on flat volume, the cost build is wrong, not the price deck [S0].

valuation.basis: average of peer median and own five-year average

bear.narrative: El Nino hits the 2027 crop as GAPKI warns (up to 3m tonnes off national output) and the CPO price gives back the 2027 spike; bought-in FFB dries up and the mill runs below capacity, so tonnes fall 5% while the bought-fruit line re-prices DOWN with the benchmark. Derived from the base cost formula, not from a revenue ratio: the FFB line is about 86% of FY2027E unit cost and the estate component is fixed, so a 20% benchmark cut takes unit cost to 0.828x (1.7415 + 11.1989 x 0.8 on 12.9404) - this is a spread business, so a price fall compresses the spread rather than collapsing EBITDA, and the estate cost, the only fixed part, does not move.

bull.narrative: The 2026-27 El Nino tightens the vegetable-oil balance into 2027, B40 to B50 biodiesel keeps the Indonesian domestic bid firm, and the mill keeps its 65% bought-FFB throughput, so the price spike lands with the bought-fruit line re-priced UP alongside it - the same base cost formula in reverse, 1.7415 + 11.1989 x 1.2 on 12.9404 = 1.172x unit cost - and the extra tonnes convert into free cash flow and dividends rather than into a wider spread alone.
